objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe the five elements of the teaching process the PTS lists (preparing a lesson for a ground or flight period, presentation methods, application by the learner, review and evaluation, and problem-based learning), explain how they fit together in one instructional period, and show how you would use them to plan, teach and close a real instrument lesson.
why: A flight instructor applicant must receive and log ground training on the fundamentals of instructing, and the list includes lesson planning [[60:340|14 CFR 61.185(a)(1)]]; flight and ground instructors and certain teachers are exempt [[60:340|14 CFR 61.185(b)]]. The AIH says the teaching process organizes material so the learner can understand it, and its steps stay the same whatever delivery method you use [[25:104|AIH 5-1]]. The FAA now places more emphasis on the instructor's role as a teacher and mentor, and the learning that takes place is a direct result of the instructor's lesson preparation, delivery, observation and assessment [[25:145|AIH 7-1]]. On the checkride, evaluators are told to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions, so be ready to walk through a real lesson, not just name the steps.

key_terms.def: The way an instructor organizes material so the learner can understand it: preparation, presentation, application and assessment. The sequence stays the same whatever delivery method is used [[25:104|AIH 5-1]]. Chapter 7 calls the last step review and evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

A step-by-step, building block progression of learning with provisions for regular review and assessments at prescribed stages [[25:107|AIH 5-4]]. It is a brief digest of the course and is used as a guide [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].
An organized outline for a single instructional period: what to do, in what order and with what procedure. A mental outline is not a lesson plan; it should be written [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].
An objective that sets measurable, reasonable standards for the learner's performance. It has three parts: description of the skill or behavior, conditions and criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].
An objective designed to develop pilot judgment and ADM, taught with dynamic, meaningful scenarios [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].
The opening of a lesson, made of three elements: attention, motivation and an overview [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].
A method based on the principle that people learn by doing, best used for mental or physical skills that require practice [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].
The flight instructor's variation of demonstration-performance. Its key transition is learner tells, instructor does [[25:176|AIH 9-6]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
The learner's use of the presented material: explaining it in a classroom, or performing the flight maneuver just demonstrated [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].
Learner self-assessment plus a detailed assessment by the instructor, followed by an in-depth discussion that compares the two [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
A learning environment where lessons involve learners with problems met in real life and ask them to find real-world solutions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
A type of problem-based instruction that uses a highly structured script of real-world experiences to address training objectives in an operational environment [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

chunks.title: The teaching process: four steps and the PTS words

body.p: This lesson follows the five items the PTS lists for the Teaching Process Task. The PTS references the older FAA-H-8083-9; this lesson teaches from the current FAA-H-8083-9B. The CFI lesson FI.I.C covers the same AIH chapters from the CFI ACS side, with more on course development and instructional aids. Here the focus is the process itself, with instrument examples. Two sibling FOI lessons go deeper on parts of it: FOI.I.D Teaching Methods covers each presentation method, and FOI.I.E Critique and Evaluation covers critiques, questions and tests.

**What teaching is.** Teaching is to instruct or train. The AIH quotes psychologist Stanford Ericksen: good teachers select and organize worthwhile material, lead learners to encode it in memorable form, ensure competence in the procedures of a discipline, sustain curiosity and promote learning on their own [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

**The process.** The teaching process organizes the material so the learner can understand it. It has four steps: preparation, presentation, application and assessment, and the overall sequence stays the same whatever delivery method you use [[25:104|AIH 5-1]]. Research found that effective instructors come in many forms, but they know how to process these four steps [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

Figure 9-7 lines the four steps up with the demonstration-performance method and the telling-and-doing technique [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Chapter 7 names the fourth step **review and evaluation**, the PTS's own words, and says every adequately developed lesson falls logically into these four steps [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

check.q: An examiner asks: 'Does the teaching process change when you switch from a lecture to a demonstration in the airplane?' What do you say?
check.a: No. The four steps (preparation, presentation, application, and assessment, also called review and evaluation) stay the same whatever delivery method is used [[25:104|AIH 5-1]] [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Only the method inside the presentation step changes.

chunks.title: Preparation I: objectives and standards come first

body.p: **Start from the course.** A course of training is a complete series of studies toward a goal such as a certificate. A syllabus outlines a course with several lessons, each with objectives and completion standards; in aviation the training syllabus is a building block progression with regular review and assessments at set stages. A lesson plan is the detailed plan for one lesson: objectives, organization of material, teaching aids, instructor and learner actions, and evaluation criteria and completion standards [[25:107|AIH 5-4]].

**Objectives and standards precede instruction.** Many instructors use a commercially developed syllabus, and its objectives are the starting point [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Objectives apply to all three domains of learning and should include the desired level of learning, and clearly defined objectives that the learner understands are essential whatever technique you use [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Standards describe the desired knowledge, behavior or skill in specific terms, with conditions and criteria; when a learner performs to well-defined standards, learning is evident [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

**Performance-based objectives** set measurable, reasonable standards for the learner's performance. They should be clear, measurable and repeatable, and mean the same thing to any knowledgeable reader [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. They have three parts [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]:

head: Part
What it is
AIH example
Instrument example (Application)
rows: Description of the skill or behavior
The desired outcome in concrete, measurable terms. Avoid 'knowledge of' and 'awareness of' [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]
'Able to select from a list of' or 'able to repeat the steps to' [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]
'Fly the published hold at the assigned fix'
Conditions
The rules for showing the skill: equipment, tools, reference material and limiting parameters. If a reader asks 'But what if...?', the conditions need work [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]
'Using appropriate charts, a prepared flight log, and training aircraft' [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]
'In the training airplane with a view-limiting device, using the en route chart and a hold clearance read by the instructor'
Criteria
The standards that measure accomplishment, so there is no question whether the performance met the objective [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]
Arrive within 5 minutes of the planned time and hold altitude within 200 feet en route [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]
'Correct entry, with altitude and airspeed within the limits briefed before flight'

body.p: **Decision-based objectives** develop judgment and ADM. With dynamic, meaningful scenarios you teach the learner to gather information and make informed, safe and timely decisions [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. As the learner reaches higher levels of performance and understanding, shift the training focus toward them [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. They do not replace maneuver training: maneuvers that need repetition are still taught in concentrated settings, then built into realistic flight situations [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

**Use the standards, but aim higher.** The ACS gives specific performance objectives for a certificate or rating [[25:109|AIH 5-6]], but ACS/PTS standards are limited to the most critical job tasks, and certification tests do not represent an entire training syllabus [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Teach not only how, but also why and when, and build ADM and risk management into each lesson [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Use the maneuver-based approach of the ACS, but present the objectives in a scenario [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

callout.text: Application: once you list the criteria for the objective, you have already written the lesson's completion standards [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. Read the objective to the learner in the briefing: the AIH says knowing the big picture and what is expected can ease a significant source of uncertainty and frustration [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

check.q: Your syllabus says: 'The learner will have knowledge of holding.' How do you fix it?
check.a: Phrases like 'knowledge of' cannot be measured very well [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. Rewrite it with a measurable behavior, the conditions (airplane or device, chart, clearance) and criteria that leave no question whether it was met [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

chunks.title: Preparation II: the written lesson plan

body.p: **A lesson plan** is an organized outline for one instructional period. It tells you what to do, in what order and with what procedure, and one should be prepared for each training period [[25:151|AIH 7-7]]. A mental outline is not a lesson plan: write it down so another instructor could take it and teach the same period, and so it can be analyzed for adequacy and completeness [[25:151|AIH 7-7]]. A well-built syllabus already holds much of a lesson plan, including objectives, content and completion standards [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

**Why bother.** Developing a plan means, in effect, that you have taught the lesson to yourself before teaching it to the learner [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. An adequate lesson plan, properly used, should [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]:

bullets: Assure a wise selection of material and drop unimportant details [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Give due consideration to each part of the lesson [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Help you present the material in a suitable sequence for efficient learning [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Outline the teaching procedure and relate the lesson to the course objectives [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].
Give the inexperienced instructor confidence, and promote uniform instruction whoever teaches it and whenever [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

body.p: **The planning cycle.** Determine the objective, then research the subject. Next choose the method of instruction and a lesson planning format, then decide how to organize the lesson and select support material. Last, assemble training aids and write the outline [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. One technique is to write the beginning and the ending first, and the plan stays a working document you revise as needed [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

body.p: **Formats.** Format depends on the subject and the method; one-on-one plans may be simple, but all should include objectives, content to support them, and completion standards [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Commercially developed lesson plans are acceptable, including for flight instructor applicants on their practical tests, but even well-designed preprinted plans may need changes [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Figure 7-3 shows a flight lesson with those three parts, including view-limiting device time and items flown by instrument reference (IR) [[25:149|AIH 7-5]].

**For instrument training,** the IFH's Instrument Training Lesson Guide arranges lessons in a logical, building-block sequence, each with ground training that fits the flight portion [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. It says it is vitally important to brief the student on the lesson objective and how it will be met, that debriefing is necessary to motivate further progress, and that students should master each lesson's objective before advancing [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. When possible, each lesson should include radio communications, basic navigation and emergency procedures, so the student meets the entire IFR experience on each flight [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

check.q: Your flight lesson plan exists only in your head because you have taught it many times. What does the AIH say?
check.a: A mental outline is not a lesson plan. Put it in writing so another instructor could conduct the same period from it and so it can be analyzed for adequacy and completeness [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

chunks.title: Preparation III: getting ready for the ground or flight period

body.p: **Ground period.** The AIH's model instructor, Bob, arrives thirty minutes early to check the room, his notes, the computer and the handouts, so he is free to greet learners as they come in [[25:104|AIH 5-1]]. Good time management means planning time for what needs to be done and for the unexpected, and not planning too much for the time you have [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]. Figure 5-6 (in the next chunk) lists what to do before, during and after a lesson [[25:111|AIH 5-8]].

For a teaching lecture, the AIH gives four planning steps: establish the objective and desired outcomes, research the subject, organize the material, and plan productive classroom activities [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]. Then rehearse it; if possible, have another instructor watch the dry run and act as critic [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

**Flight period.** The instructor must plan the flight to the same extent as the learner who prepares for it, and flight instruction needs objectives and a syllabus paired with the ground instruction already given [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. Even when the learner has had ground school on a task, review that task with the learner before flight [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. Relate ground training objectives to flight training objectives whenever possible, and point out the link between theory and practice [[25:172|AIH 9-2]].

The explanation phase happens before the flight: discuss the objectives and completion standards, give a thorough preflight briefing, and cover the safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. The preflight briefing should include the procedure for exchanging the flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Before any flight, also discuss safety and the importance of a proper preflight and use of the checklist [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

**Know the learner.** A lesson plan for a flight period should fit the learner's background, flight experience and ability [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Learning the learner's aviation background lets you plan blocks that build on what the learner already knows [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

callout.text: Application, a night-before checklist for an instrument flight lesson: objective and completion standards written; a ground review planned for what was taught in ground school [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]; briefing points ready, including safety procedures and how you will exchange the controls [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; and, for flexibility, room for add-on material [[25:152|AIH 7-8]], such as a spare task if the weather changes the plan.

check.q: Your learner had two hours of ground school on holding last week. Can you skip the ground review before today's holding flight?
check.a: No. Even when the learner has received ground school on a task, the instructor should review that same task with the learner before flight [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

body.p: Presentation is where you deliver the lesson and hold the learner's attention. Figure 5-6 gives the AIH's guidelines, and many of them can be combined during a real presentation [[25:111|AIH 5-8]].
**Organization.** The traditional organization of a lesson plan is introduction, development and conclusion [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].
**Introduction: attention, motivation, overview** [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

bullets: **Attention** focuses each learner on the lesson: a story, a video clip, a question or a joke. It should relate to the subject; something unrelated distracts from the lesson [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

**Motivation** gives specific reasons why the content is important to know or perform, which ensures readiness (Thorndike's law of readiness). Examples of someone applying the knowledge, or a reminder of an upcoming assessment, both work [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].
**Overview** tells what will be covered: a clear, concise presentation of the objective and the key ideas gives the learners a road map [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

body.p: **Development** is the main part of the lesson. Organize the main points in one of four patterns [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]:

head: Pattern
AIH example
Instrument example
rows: Past to present
Tracing the development of radio navigation systems [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
Application: use it when history explains why a procedure is built the way it is
Simple-to-complex
Leave Class A, B and C airspace until the learner is familiar with D, E and G [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
The IFH says cross-check and interpretation are learned separately and in deliberate sequence, and a measure of proficiency is the ability to integrate them [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]
Known to unknown
Teach the magnetic compass before gyroscopic heading indicators [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]
The IFH suggests demonstrating pitch corrections by comparing the attitude indicator with the natural horizon [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]
Most frequently used to least used
Teach basic navigation before a computerized navigation system, since all pilots use the basic skills [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]

body.p: Under each main point, the subpoints should lead naturally from one to the next. Clear transitions keep learners oriented and help them sort and remember what they are taught [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

**Conclusion.** Retrace the important elements and relate them to the objective; this review reinforces learning and improves retention. Do not introduce new ideas in the conclusion, because they are likely to confuse [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Repeating key points at the end of a lesson uses the principle of recency [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

check.q: You open a partial panel ground lesson with a funny story about your airline simulator check that has nothing to do with instruments. What is wrong?
check.a: The attention element should relate to the subject and set up the learning outcomes; a story or joke unrelated to the subject distracts from the lesson [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

body.p: **The choices.** You can present material by lecture, discussion, guided discussion, problem-based learning, group learning, demonstration-performance or e-learning, and an effective instructor normally combines methods in a typical lesson [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. In the AIH's opening scenario, Bob lectures on weight and balance, then uses group learning to reinforce the lecture [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. The setting and purpose of each lesson decide which method you use [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].
The lesson FOI.I.D Teaching Methods covers each method in depth. At the level of the teaching process, know what each is good for:

head: Method
What it is good for
Instrument training example (Application)
rows: Lecture

A general understanding of a subject, and common background for learners with varied backgrounds [[25:113|AIH 5-10]] [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. It gives no precise measure of understanding and does not build motor skills [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
A short talk on how an ILS is built, before the device session
Discussion
A short lecture followed by instructor-learner and learner-learner discussion; it improves recall and helps develop HOTS [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
Two learners compare how they would brief the same approach chart
Guided discussion
Drawing out the learner's knowledge with the instructor in control; usable in classrooms and in preflight and postflight briefings [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
A lead-off 'why' question about hold entries [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]

Real-world problems with no single solution [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]

Demonstration-performance

body.p: **Lecture limits.** A learner's retention drops off significantly after the first 10-15 minutes of a lecture and improves at the end, so adding active learner participation in the middle greatly increases retention [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].
**Drill and practice** rests on Thorndike's law of exercise: connections are strengthened with practice, and learners do not master crosswind landings in one flight [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

**E-learning cautions.** Avoid improper or excessive use: do not rely only on a software program for patterns and landings and then expect the learner to fly them in the aircraft [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. The computer has no way of knowing when a learner is having difficulty, so monitoring progress is always your job [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. The AIH says studies have shown that learners who use electronic media extensively are generally not as well trained as those who get a balanced mix of methods [[25:172|AIH 9-2]].

**Instructional aids** support, supplement or reinforce what is being taught; they are not self-supporting. An aid should keep the learner's attention on the subject, not be a distracting gimmick [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

callout.text: The instructor's success is determined to a large degree by the ability to organize material and to select and use a teaching method suited to the particular lesson [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

check.q: Your learner has flown every approach in a home simulator program. Can you skip the ground and flight presentation on approaches?
check.a: No. The AIH warns against relying only on software for ground instruction and then expecting performance in the aircraft, and says the computer cannot know when a learner is having difficulty [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

chunks.title: Presentation III: explaining and demonstrating in the airplane

body.p: Flight instructors use demonstration-performance for procedures and maneuvers because it is very effective for kinesthetic skills [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Chapter 9 gives it four phases: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Chapter 5 counts learner performance and instructor supervision separately, for five phases [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

**Explanation.** Done before the flight lesson, it covers objectives, completion standards and a thorough preflight briefing. Give clear objectives based on the learner's known experience, convey the precise actions to perform, describe the end result, cover safety procedures, and invite questions on any step not understood [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

**Demonstration.** Show the actions, and you may describe them at the same time. Avoid extraneous activity. If the demonstration does not closely match the explanation, acknowledge and explain the deviation right away [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

**Instructor tells, instructor does** is the first step of the telling-and-doing technique and the only step where the learner plays a passive role. Explain the power settings, attitudes and other factors as you fly, and demonstrate in the same sequence as the explanation [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Learners generally imitate the instructor, so demonstrate exactly the way they should practice, including all safety procedures [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Avoid jargon the learner does not know; trying to impress learners with complicated language is neither appropriate nor effective [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

callout.text: Application, an instrument demonstration from the IFH: an instructor pilot can demonstrate an excessive nose-down deviation and then show the result of improper corrective technique. The normal impulse is a large pitch correction in a hurry, which leads to overcontrolling; the correct technique is slower and smoother and returns the airplane to the desired attitude more quickly [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Say clearly which version is wrong and which is right.

body.p: **Integrated training curricula.** For an ILS, the AIH describes teaching the required knowledge in the classroom, then the flight procedures, then the psychomotor skills in a simulator, where the instructor demonstrates and teaches the approach; when the learner is proficient there, training moves to the aircraft to verify proficiency [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. The FAA recommends that simulator training continue until the tasks are accomplished successfully before they are tried in an aircraft [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

**Model it.** Individuals learn by observing others, so model safe and professional behavior at all times [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Teach the concept of a sterile flight deck and model it during flight instruction [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: During your demonstration of a climbing turn under the hood you overshoot the heading. What should you do?
check.a: Acknowledge and explain the deviation right away, because the demonstration should conform to the explanation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Learners imitate the instructor, so do not let a flawed demonstration pass without comment [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

chunks.title: Application I: the learner explains and performs

body.p: **What application is.** Application is the learner's use of the presented material. In a classroom the learner may be asked to explain the new material; with a new flight maneuver, to perform the maneuver just demonstrated [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. In most lessons your explanation and demonstration alternate with the learner's attempts, and you usually offer corrections and further demonstrations [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

**Right from the start.** Each learner needs to perform the maneuver the right way the first few times to establish a good habit. Faulty habits are difficult to correct and need to be addressed as soon as possible [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. Learners often practice without an instructor, so periodic review and assessment are needed, and learners should practice maneuvers on solo flights only after showing reasonable competence [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. This is primacy: what is learned first often creates a strong, almost unshakable impression [[25:64|AIH 3-13]].

**Soon after the demonstration.** Give the learner a chance to perform the skill as soon as possible after a demonstration. In flight, the learner may follow along on the controls during your demonstration and then try the maneuver right away, with coaching as needed [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]. Learner performance and instructor supervision happen at the same time, and you must allot enough time for meaningful activity [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
**Telling-and-doing: the learner takes over in steps** [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]:

bullets: **Learner tells, instructor does.** The learner plays the instructor and tells you what to do while you fly. Freed from flying, she can organize her thoughts about the steps, and you can evaluate her understanding. A misunderstanding can be corrected before she becomes absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Figure 9-7 marks this as the key transition [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

**Learner tells, learner does.** This is application, where learning takes place and performance habits form. She thinks aloud while flying, which focuses her concentration and shows you whether an error comes from a misconception or a simple lack of motor skills [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
**Learner does, instructor evaluates** is the last row of Figure 9-7, the evaluation step [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

callout.text: Application, a talk-through for a standard rate level turn to a heading under the hood, built from the IFH's steps: first have her tell you each step while you fly it (roll in with coordinated aileron and rudder, using the attitude indicator to set the approximate bank and then the turn coordinator to confirm standard rate; check the altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator for pitch as the vertical lift component decreases; trim off the pressures once the bank is set; practice leading the rollout by one-half the bank angle) [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. The AIH's own level turn talk-through is written for a visual turn, with outside references [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], so swap in the instrument references. Then she flies it while saying the same steps. If she forgets to trim, fix it early: the IFH says poor trim is one of the most common errors instructors note in instrument students [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].

check.q: Your learner flies her first partial panel turn well but cannot say why she led the rollout. Which telling-and-doing step did you probably skip?
check.a: Learner tells, instructor does. It lets her organize her thoughts about the steps and lets you evaluate her understanding before she is busy controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Application II: supervising, correcting and handing over decisions

body.p: **How much help.** How much control you use depends on the learner's proficiency, the type of maneuver and the stage of training. With hazardous or difficult maneuvers, especially on a first attempt, be ready to take control at any time; with a learner progressing normally, avoid unnecessary interruptions or too much assistance [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Let the learner practice the entire maneuver often enough to reach the proficiency in the lesson objectives. This is a learning phase, not an evaluation phase, so correct errors in a positive and timely way, and schedule more training if the standard is not met in the time allotted [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

**Correcting errors.** Correction does not mean taking over the moment a mistake is made. Safety permitting, it is often better to let learners go part way into the mistake and find a way out; it is hard to learn a maneuver if learners seldom get to correct an error [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

**Checking understanding.** A learner may fly a maneuver correctly without understanding its principles. If you suspect this, have the learner vary the maneuver slightly, combine it with other operations, or apply the same elements to other maneuvers; a learner who does not understand probably cannot do this [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

**Positive exchange of flight controls** is especially critical during demonstration-performance. Brief the procedure before flight and use the three-step exchange, with a visual check that the other pilot actually has the controls; there should never be any doubt about who is flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. When necessary, take the controls and calmly announce, 'I have the flight controls.' If a recovery is needed, nothing is gained by having the learner on the controls and fighting for them [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

**Toward decisions.** As the learner becomes proficient, emphasize ADM more and more as the way to apply what was learned. The AIH's example: the learner plans the arrival at a specific nontowered airport, then makes the decisions to enter and fly the pattern, with guidance and feedback as necessary [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

callout.text: Distractions belong in application. Most stall/spin accidents occurred when the pilot's attention was diverted, and the most effective training simulates scenarios that can lead to inadvertent stalls by creating distractions while the learner practices certain maneuvers [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Learners should never be allowed to exceed your limits as the instructor [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: On her third hold, your learner starts the outbound turn the wrong way at the fix. The airplane is stable, traffic is clear and she is well above any minimum altitude. What does the AIH suggest?
check.a: Safety permitting, let her go part way into the mistake and find her way out, because learners need chances to correct errors [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Be ready to take control at once if it becomes hazardous [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Review and evaluation I: closing the lesson

body.p: **Assessment of the lesson.** Before the end of the period, review what was covered and ask the learner to show how well the lesson objectives were met. Review and assessment are integral parts of each classroom or flight lesson [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. The assessment may be informal and recorded only for your own planning of the next lesson, or formal and recorded to certify progress [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

**Evaluation in flight training.** The instructor traditionally evaluates the learner's performance, records it, and tells the learner the progress made toward the objectives. When pointing out areas to improve, offer concrete suggestions that help, and if possible do not end on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Determine to what extent the learner met the objectives set in the preflight discussion [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
**Assessment by timing** [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]:

bullets: **Diagnostic:** before a course of instruction [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. The IFH lesson guide opens with Lesson 1, a ground and flight evaluation of the student's knowledge and performance [[23:342|IFH B-1]].
**Formative:** not graded; it wraps up the lesson, sets the stage for the next one, and tells you what to reinforce [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].
**Summative:** used periodically to measure how far learning has progressed, such as a stage check, a chapter quiz or an end-of-course test [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

body.p: **After the flight,** review or discuss flight events and choices using ADM principles, and plan remediation if trends show an inadequate skill, a hazardous attitude or inadequate knowledge of risk mitigation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Keep the learner informed of progress, after each maneuver or in the postflight critique, and use written notes so you cover everything you noticed [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. In the first stages of a skill, practical suggestions are worth more to the learner than a grade [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

**Recency and the record.** Instructors use the principle of recency when they plan the summary of a ground lesson or a postflight critique, repeating the important points at the end [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]. Lesson plans make good recordkeeping forms, with room to mark what was completed, the date, your signature, time flown and comments [[25:151|AIH 7-7]], and the AIH recommends a training folder for each learner, kept at least 3 years [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

check.q: You land 15 minutes late and your next learner is waiting. Can you skip the review and just say 'good job'?
check.a: No. Review and assessment are integral parts of each lesson and come before the period ends [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. Keep it short but specific, record it, and use it to plan the next lesson [[25:126|AIH 5-23]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Review and evaluation II: judging performance with the learner

body.p: **Assessment of piloting ability.** Assessment determines how, what and how well a learner is learning. A well-designed one gives the learner something constructive to work on and direction to raise performance. Learners must understand its purpose, or they will be unlikely to accept it [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Flight instructors generally use the review, collaborative assessment (LCG), written tests and performance-based tests [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

**Judge against standards, suitably modified.** Assessment of demonstrated ability must be based on established standards of performance, modified to fit the learner's experience and stage of development, and it must consider mastery of the elements of the maneuver, not merely the overall performance [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed those in the ACS/PTS before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

**Reteach when it helps.** If you see a deficiency that needs reteaching, demonstrate the maneuver, let the learner practice it under direction, then evaluate by watching the performance [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

**Collaborative assessment.** Traditional scales such as 'excellent, good, fair, poor' often meet the instructor's needs but not the learner's, and with SBT, collaborative assessment is used whenever the learner completes a scenario [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. It has two parts: the learner's self-assessment, then a detailed assessment by the instructor, followed by an in-depth discussion that compares the two [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Guide the self-assessment with four steps of open-ended questions: replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. Progress can then be placed on the maneuver grades (describe, explain, practice, perform, not observed) and the risk management grades (explain, practice, manage-decide) [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].
As the learner grows in flight knowledge, she should be able to lead the postflight review while you guide the discussion with targeted questions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].

callout.text: An effective assessment is objective, flexible, acceptable, comprehensive, constructive, organized, thoughtful and specific [[25:133|AIH 6-2]] [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]. FOI.I.E covers these, the critique methods, oral questions and tests in depth.

check.q: After an approach scenario your learner rates himself 'Perform'. You saw him need two prompts on the missed approach. What happens next?
check.a: Discuss the difference: in collaborative assessment the self-assessment is followed by an in-depth discussion comparing your assessment with his [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. 'Perform' means doing the activity without instructor assistance, while needing coaching fits 'Practice' [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

chunks.title: Problem-based learning I: real problems, no single answer

body.p: **Origin and definition.** In 1966 the McMaster University School of Medicine in Canada pioneered problem-based learning (PBL), and it has helped shift learning from instructor-centered to learner-centered. The AIH defines it as a learning environment where lessons involve learners with problems encountered in real life and ask them to find real-world solutions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].

PBL starts with a carefully constructed problem that has no single solution. It helps the learner understand the information more deeply and recall it better, and it builds HOTS: problem solving, decision-making, analysis, synthesis and evaluation [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
**Effective problems** [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]:

bullets: Relate to the real world, so learners want to solve them [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
Require learners to make decisions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
Are open-ended, not limited to one correct answer [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
Connect to previously learned knowledge as well as new knowledge [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
Reflect the lesson objectives [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].
Challenge learners to think critically [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].

body.p: **Teaching HOTS.** Build analysis, synthesis and evaluation into lessons with PBL, from simple to complex and from concrete to abstract, throughout the curriculum [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. The AIH's basic approach: set up the problem; determine learning outcomes; solve it; reflect on the process; consider other solutions through guided discovery; reevaluate with the new options; reflect on why this could be the best solution; and consider what 'best' means [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

A problem-based lesson usually includes a need to solve the problem, a decision on how to find a solution, a possible solution, an explanation of the reasons for it, and reflection on the solution [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

callout.text: Application, an instrument problem built to the six traits: 'You are flying your family to a wedding 200 miles away in the training airplane. The forecast at your arrival time is close to your personal minimums. Plan the trip and tell me what would make you change it.' It is real, needs decisions, has several good answers, builds on what she knows, matches an IFR cross-country objective and makes her think [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].

check.q: Is 'List the holding entry rules' a good PBL problem?
check.a: No. It has one correct answer and needs no decision. Effective problems relate to the real world, require decisions, are open-ended, connect old and new knowledge, reflect the objective and challenge critical thinking [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].

chunks.title: Problem-based learning II: SBT, collaborative problem-solving and case studies

body.p: The AIH gives three types of problem-based instruction: scenario-based, collaborative problem-solving and case study [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

**Scenario-based training (SBT)** uses a highly structured script of real-world experiences to address training objectives in an operational environment, and its scenarios require the pilot to manage resources, use sound judgment and make timely decisions [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. A scenario may not have one right answer, so know in advance which outcomes are positive and negative, and give the learner freedom to make both good and poor decisions without jeopardizing safety [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. A good flight scenario begins with a reason to fly, because a pilot's decisions differ with the motivation to fly [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

A good scenario is not a test, will not have one right answer, does not offer an obvious answer, should not promote errors, and should promote situational awareness and chances to make decisions [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

**Collaborative problem-solving.** Give a group a problem and help only when needed, since learning to solve it without help is part of the learning. One-on-one, give the learner the problem and offer limited help as she solves it [[25:121|AIH 5-18]].

**Case study.** A real-life story the learner analyzes to reach conclusions and possible solutions. NTSB accident descriptions are an excellent source: remove the probable cause, let learners discuss causes without bias, then share the NTSB's determination [[25:121|AIH 5-18]].

**Traditional and SBT lesson plans.** With the traditional plan in Figure 7-6, the learner ends the lesson able to practice the maneuver only with the instructor's help [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. With the SBT plan in Figure 7-7, the learner plans an arrival at a specific nontowered airport, flies it, then discusses what was done, why, the consequences, other courses of action and how it applies to other airports; the learner ends able to detail a safe arrival at any nontowered airport in a variety of winds [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].

**Pre-scenario planning.** For a flight scenario, set the destination, desired learning outcomes, desired level of performance and possible in-flight scenario changes [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. Turn planning and execution of the flight over to the learner as soon as possible, and when the learner begins to make decisions, revert to the role of mentor and learning facilitator [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. Maneuvers that need repetition are still taught in concentrated settings, then built into realistic flight situations [[25:154|AIH 7-10]].

**Visualization.** Have the learner describe how the flight should go, then add an unforeseen change; for instrument airplane learners the AIH suggests radio outages. Ask questions to check her thinking, and challenge her with realistic situations without overburdening, unrealistic scenarios [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

check.q: You plan to fail the radio, the vacuum system and the alternator on one approach to 'see what she does'. What does the AIH say?
check.a: Challenge the learner with realistic situations without creating overburdening, unrealistic scenarios [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. A good scenario is not a test and should not promote errors [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

chunks.title: Risks: where the teaching process breaks down

body.p: Each step can fail in a way that costs the learner time, money or safety. The table pairs common breakdowns with the AIH's fix.

Breakdown you may see

rows: Preparation
Teaching from a mental outline, so points get skipped and irrelevant material creeps in
Write the plan and use it as a guide; it keeps you from getting off track, omitting essential points and adding irrelevant material [[25:151|AIH 7-7]] [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]
Preparation
Teaching only to the checkride tolerances
The ACS/PTS is a testing tool, not a teaching tool; focus on why the standards are there [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]

A long lecture with no learner activity
Retention drops after the first 10-15 minutes; add active participation in the middle [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
Presentation

Acknowledge and explain the deviation right away [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]

The instructor flies most of the period and practice is squeezed in at the end
Let the learner perform as soon as possible after a demonstration, and allot enough time for meaningful activity [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]

Correct early; faulty habits are difficult to correct [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]
Review and evaluation
No time for a debrief, or only a vague 'good job'
Review before the period ends, and make comments specific [[25:126|AIH 5-23]] [[25:134|AIH 6-3]]
Problem-based learning

A good scenario is not a test, has no obvious answer and does not promote errors [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]

callout.text: Safety comes before teaching. Instructors should not exceed their own ability to perceive a problem, decide on a course of action and physically react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Plan scenarios so the learner can make poor decisions without jeopardizing safety [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

body.p: **How it is tested.** The PTS NOTE for Area I has the evaluator select at least Tasks E, F and G and one other, so this Task may or may not be chosen. Its objective verb is describing, and evaluators are told to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions when possible (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I and Introduction). Expect questions such as 'Walk me through how you would prepare and teach a first lesson on holding' or 'Your learner flies the maneuver well but cannot explain it. What do you do?'

check.q: The examiner says: 'Your lesson plan had the learner doing three approaches, two holds and partial panel in one hour. What would you change?'
check.a: The scope. Each lesson should be reasonable in scope: too much material confuses, too little is inefficient [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. Split it into lessons with limited objectives, each a unified segment [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

scenario.title: First ILS in the airplane
scenario.setup: Dana is a private pilot with 210 hours, working on her instrument rating with you under part 61 in a four-seat trainer. She has flown the ILS at your home airport twice in the school's advanced training device and chased the glideslope both times. Tomorrow is her first ILS in the airplane, and the forecast is VFR with a gusty crosswind. She works full time, studies at night with an app, and goes quiet when she makes mistakes. Next month she wants to fly a real IFR trip to see her parents.

questions.q: How do you prepare tomorrow's lesson?
questions.a: Start from the syllabus objective and write it as a performance-based objective with conditions and criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. Put the plan in writing with objectives, content and completion standards [[25:151|AIH 7-7]] [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Keep the scope reasonable and relate it to her course and her trip home [[25:152|AIH 7-8]] [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Plan the flight as thoroughly as you expect her to [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

questions.q: What goes into the preflight briefing?
questions.a: The explanation phase: objectives and completion standards, the precise actions and the end result, safety procedures, and time for questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], plus how you will exchange the flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Review the ILS on the ground even though she flew it in the device [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]; the IFH lists chasing the CDI and glidepath needles as an ILS error, especially when the approach was not studied enough before the flight [[23:285|IFH 9-42]]. Use her trip home as the motivation element, which ensures readiness [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

questions.q: Which presentation methods do you combine, and in what order?
questions.a: A short guided discussion on the ground to draw out what she knows about the ILS [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. In the air, instructor tells, instructor does, then learner tells, instructor does, so she talks you through an approach before she flies one [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. That fits the AIH's integrated sequence of classroom, device, then airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

questions.q: On her first approach she makes large, hurried pitch corrections and goes above and below the glideslope. What do you do during application?
questions.a: Safety permitting, let her work part way into the error and out of it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], then name it: the IFH lists chasing the CDI and glidepath needles as a common ILS error [[23:285|IFH 9-42]], and its level-flight pitch demonstration shows that a large pitch correction made in a hurry leads to overcontrolling, while slower, smoother technique returns to the desired attitude more quickly [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Have her think aloud on the next approach so you can tell a misconception from a motor skill gap [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Correct it early, before it becomes a habit [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

questions.q: How do you close the lesson, knowing she goes quiet after mistakes?
questions.a: Review before the period ends and check the objectives [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. Use collaborative assessment: her replay, reconstruct, reflect and redirect, then your assessment and a discussion comparing the two [[25:136|AIH 6-5]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Give concrete suggestions and try not to end on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Record it and use it to plan the next lesson [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

questions.q: How could her trip home become a problem-based lesson later in training?
questions.a: Build an SBT scenario that starts with that reason to fly, with good and poor outcomes known to you in advance and no single right answer [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. Set the destination, outcomes, desired performance and possible changes before the flight [[25:155|AIH 7-11]], and add a realistic twist such as a radio outage without overloading her [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

skills.do: Describe aloud how you prepare one ground period and one flight period: the objective and its three parts, the written plan and its characteristics, the planning cycle, and what you do before the learner arrives or before engine start.
skills.practice: Pick one lesson from the IFH Instrument Training Lesson Guide, such as Lesson 6, Partial panel operations [[23:343|IFH B-2]], and write a one-page plan with objectives, content and completion standards [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Brief it to a study partner in five minutes, including how you will exchange the controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], and ask the partner to test the conditions with 'But what if...?' questions [[25:109|AIH 5-6]].

skills.do: Explain problem-based learning and its three types, then build and walk through an instrument scenario that meets the AIH's traits for an effective problem and a good scenario.
skills.practice: Write one IFR scenario that starts with a reason to fly. List the good and poor outcomes you expect and the changes you may add, then check it against the six traits of an effective problem and the five traits of a good scenario [[25:119|AIH 5-16]] [[25:120|AIH 5-17]] [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. Run it with a partner as a visualization, then close with a collaborative assessment [[25:183|AIH 9-13]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Your instrument learner asks why you write a lesson plan for holds you have taught many times. Which statement matches the AIH?
options: A mental outline is enough for any lesson you know well
Written plans are only needed for ground school
It lets another instructor teach the same period
Only a part 141 school syllabus calls for written plans
quiz.why: A mental outline is not a lesson plan. It should be written so another instructor could conduct the same period and so it can be analyzed for adequacy and completeness [[25:151|AIH 7-7]]. Plans should be prepared for each training period, ground or flight, so the ground-school-only idea is wrong [[25:151|AIH 7-7]].

quiz.q: In this objective, which part is the criteria? 'Using the approach chart and the training device, fly the RNAV approach to minimums, staying within the course and altitude limits briefed before the session.'
options: Using the approach chart and the training device
Fly the RNAV approach to minimums
The level of learning that the syllabus names for this lesson
Staying within the briefed course and altitude limits
quiz.why: Criteria are the standards that measure accomplishment, so there is no question whether the objective was met [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. The chart and device are conditions [[25:109|AIH 5-6]], and 'fly the approach' is the description of the behavior [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

quiz.q: Which description of the skill or behavior should you avoid when writing a performance-based objective?
options: Knowledge of holding pattern entries
Able to select the hold entry from a diagram
Able to repeat the steps to copy a hold clearance
Able to fly the entry chosen for the assigned fix
quiz.why: Phrases such as 'knowledge of' and 'awareness of' cannot be measured very well and should be avoided. Phrases like 'able to select from a list of' or 'able to repeat the steps to' describe something measurable [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

quiz.q: When does the AIH say to shift the training focus toward decision-based objectives?
options: After the learner passes the instrument practical test
As the learner reaches higher levels of performance
From the first lesson, in place of maneuvers
Only within a part 141 approved syllabus
quiz.why: As the learner progresses through higher levels of performance and understanding, the instructor should shift the focus to decision-based objectives [[25:108|AIH 5-5]]. They do not replace maneuver training from the first lesson: maneuvers that need repetition are still taught, then built into scenarios [[25:110|AIH 5-7]].

quiz.q: Right after the attention step, you tell your learner that partial panel will be on her checkride and could save her life someday. Which introduction element is that, and what does it ensure?
options: Overview; it gives the road map
Attention; it focuses the learner
Motivation; it ensures readiness
Development; it links main points
quiz.why: The motivation element gives specific reasons why the content is important, such as an upcoming assessment, and ensures readiness (Thorndike's law of readiness) [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]. The overview presents the objective and key ideas as a road map, and attention was the step before [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

quiz.q: Before teaching your learner the GPS navigator, you teach basic navigation because every pilot uses it. Which development pattern is that?
options: Most frequently used to least used
Known to unknown
Simple-to-complex
Past to present
quiz.why: This is the AIH's own example of the most-frequently-used-to-least-used pattern: begin with basic navigation, since all pilots use the basic skills [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Known to unknown also sounds right, but its AIH example starts from something the learner already knows, the magnetic compass [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

quiz.q: With five minutes left in a holding ground lesson, a learner asks about DME arcs. What belongs in your conclusion?
options: A first look at DME arcs while time remains
Retrace the key points and tie them to the objective
A short quiz on the approach material planned for next week
Only the homework assignment for next time
quiz.why: An effective conclusion retraces the important elements and relates them to the objective. New ideas should not be introduced in the conclusion because they are likely to confuse [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Note the arc question and answer it in a later lesson.

quiz.q: Why does the AIH want a learner to perform a new maneuver the right way the first few times?
options: Recency makes the first try last longest
The ACS grades only the first attempt
So solo practice can begin that day
Faulty habits are hard to correct
quiz.why: Each learner needs to perform the maneuver the right way the first few times to establish a good habit, and faulty habits are difficult to correct [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. That is primacy, not recency: what is learned first creates a strong impression [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]. Solo practice should come only after reasonable competence [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

quiz.q: Which telling-and-doing step lets you check the learner's understanding before she is busy flying?
options: Instructor tells, instructor does
Learner tells, instructor does
Learner tells, learner does
Learner does, instructor evaluates
quiz.why: In learner tells, instructor does, the learner organizes her thoughts while you fly, you can evaluate her understanding, and a misunderstanding is corrected before she becomes absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Figure 9-7 calls it the key transition [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

quiz.q: On her second approach your learner starts to drift off the localizer. The airplane is stable and safe. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Let her go part way into it and recover
Take the controls at once and show the fix
Call out each correction so she never drifts
Stop the approach and debrief it on the ground
quiz.why: Correction of errors does not mean taking over immediately. Safety permitting, it is often better to let learners progress part way into the mistake and find a way out, since they rarely learn a maneuver if they seldom get to correct an error [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: When should you review the lesson and have the learner show how well the objectives were met?
options: At the start of the next lesson only
Only at the stage checks
Only when the learner asks for feedback
Before the instructional period ends
quiz.why: Before the end of the period, review what was covered and ask the learner to demonstrate how well the objectives were met; review and assessment are integral parts of each lesson [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. Stage checks are summative assessments, but they do not replace the review in every lesson [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

quiz.q: Your learner has just finished a scenario. In collaborative assessment, what comes first?
options: Your detailed grade, then her comments
A written test on the scenario's decisions
The learner's self-assessment
A pass or fail call like a checkride
quiz.why: Collaborative assessment starts with the learner's self-assessment and follows with the instructor's detailed assessment and an in-depth discussion comparing the two [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. The learner cannot flunk a lesson; the grades describe a level of performance [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

quiz.q: This is the AIH's traditional lesson plan for wind drift. Per the AIH, what can the learner do at the end of such a lesson?
options: Fly it solo to the ACS standards
Explain it in any wind condition
Teach the maneuver to another learner
Practice the maneuver only with help
quiz.why: At the end of the traditional lesson the learner is only capable of practicing the maneuver with assistance from the instructor [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Explaining a safe arrival in any wind is the outcome of the SBT lesson plan [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].

quiz.q: Which task best fits the AIH's traits of an effective problem for problem-based learning?
options: Plan a family trip as the forecast worsens
Name the holding entry rules in order
Fly three ILS approaches to the same runway
Answer a quiz with one right answer each
quiz.why: Effective problems relate to the real world, require decisions, are open-ended rather than limited to one correct answer, and challenge learners to think critically [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. A rules list and a one-answer quiz have single answers, and repeated approaches are drill, not a problem [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: An examiner asks for the four steps of the teaching process as the AIH gives them in its chapter on the teaching process. Which answer is right?
options: Explanation, demonstration, performance, evaluation
Preparation, presentation, application, assessment
Attention, motivation, overview, conclusion
Introduction, development, review, critique
final_quiz.why: The teaching process has four steps: preparation, presentation, application and assessment [[25:104|AIH 5-1]]; Chapter 7 calls the last one review and evaluation [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. Explanation and demonstration are phases of the demonstration-performance method [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], and attention, motivation and overview make up a lesson introduction [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your lesson plan for one hour covers holds, DME arcs, two approaches and partial panel. Which characteristic of a well-planned lesson does it break?
options: Practicality
Flexibility
Scope
Relation to course of training
final_quiz.why: Each lesson should be reasonable in scope: a person can master only a few principles or skills at a time, and too much material results in confusion [[25:152|AIH 7-8]]. Practicality is about the conditions and aids, and flexibility is room for add-on material [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: Twenty minutes into a holding flight, your learner cannot hold altitude in level turns. What does the AIH say about the lesson plan?
options: Finish it to keep the syllabus on time
Skip ahead to next lesson's items
Hold the review for the next flight
Change it, or drop it for review
final_quiz.why: A flight lesson plan may have to be modified considerably in flight because of deficiencies in knowledge or mastery, and in some cases the entire plan may have to be abandoned in favor of review [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants to train only to the instrument ACS tolerances. What does the AIH say?
options: The ACS/PTS is a testing tool, not a teaching tool
The ACS is the complete syllabus for the rating
Lesson standards should match the ACS from day one
Teach only how; why and when are never tested
final_quiz.why: The ACS/PTS is not a teaching tool but a testing tool, and lesson completion standards should gradually reach or exceed it before final checkride preparation [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. ACS standards cover only the most critical job tasks and are not an entire syllabus, and good instructors teach how, why and when [[25:108|AIH 5-5]].

final_quiz.q: You have written a lecture on IFR clearances. What does the AIH recommend before you give it?
options: Memorize it to deliver it word for word
Read it from a script to stay accurate
Cut the examples to fit in more facts
Rehearse it with another instructor as critic
final_quiz.why: After planning, rehearse the lecture to build confidence, ideally with another instructor observing as critic [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]. A good teaching lecture is extemporaneous, not read or memorized [[25:115|AIH 5-12]], and examples and personal experiences support the points [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: You are teaching a partial panel compass turn. Which method does the AIH say is best for skills that require practice?
options: Lecture
Demonstration-performance
Guided discussion
Case study
final_quiz.why: Demonstration-performance is best used for the mastery of mental or physical skills that require practice [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. A lecture does not foster motor skills that need hands-on practice [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner has flown many hours of approaches in a phone simulator program. What does the AIH say about relying on it?
options: Credit it fully toward the approach block
Use it in place of your ground instruction
Do not lean on it alone for airplane skills
Let its scores show readiness for the test
final_quiz.why: Avoid improper or excessive use of e-learning: do not rely exclusively on software for ground instruction and then expect the learner to perform in the aircraft [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. The computer cannot know when a learner is having difficulty, so monitoring progress stays your job [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: For a new ILS block in an integrated training program, what order does the AIH describe?
options: Classroom, then simulator, then airplane
Airplane, then simulator to fix the errors
Simulator only; skills transfer
Classroom, airplane, then simulator review
final_quiz.why: The AIH's ILS example: knowledge in the classroom, procedures, then psychomotor practice in the simulator, then the aircraft to verify proficiency [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. The FAA recommends simulator training continue until the tasks are accomplished before trying them in an aircraft [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

final_quiz.q: During your demonstration of a climbing turn under the hood you overshoot the heading. What should you do?
options: Keep going and hope it was not seen
Repeat it quietly until it looks right
Blame the turbulence and move on
Acknowledge and explain it right away
final_quiz.why: If the demonstration does not closely conform to the explanation, the deviation should be immediately acknowledged and explained [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Learners imitate the instructor, so a silent flawed demonstration teaches the flaw [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner thinks aloud as she flies the hold. Besides focusing her, what does that give you?
options: It takes the place of the postflight debrief
It meets a talk-through rule in the ACS
It shows whether an error is a misconception or a skill gap
It lets you leave out your demonstration
final_quiz.why: In learner tells, learner does, thinking aloud focuses concentration and lets you see the learner's thought processes, so it is easy to tell whether an error is induced by a misconception or a simple lack of motor skills [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Evaluation still follows [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies a perfect hold at the home VOR. How do you check that she understands the principles?
options: Have her fly the same hold three more times
Have her vary it, combine it or apply it
Ask her to recite the entry rules again
Give it a Perform grade and move on
final_quiz.why: When you suspect a learner performs correctly without understanding, require her to vary the maneuver slightly, combine it with other operations, or apply its elements to other maneuvers [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Repeating the same hold or reciting rules shows memory, not understanding.

final_quiz.q: The IFH lesson guide begins with a ground and flight evaluation of the new student's knowledge and performance. What kind of assessment is that?
options: Diagnostic
Formative
Summative
Collaborative
final_quiz.why: Diagnostic assessments assess knowledge or skills before a course of instruction [[25:132|AIH 6-1]], which is what IFH Lesson 1 does [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. Formative assessments wrap up a lesson, and summative ones measure progress periodically, such as a stage check [[25:132|AIH 6-1]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AIH prefer collaborative assessment to an 'excellent, good, fair, poor' grade after a scenario?
options: That scale is not allowed in part 61 training
Grades must use the ACS or PTS wording
Collaborative assessment takes less time
That scale fits the instructor more than the learner
final_quiz.why: Traditional scales often meet the instructor's needs but not the learner's, and collaborative assessment is used whenever the learner completes a scenario [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. The AIH says instructors may think it takes more time, when it is really a more structured version of the traditional critique [[25:138|AIH 6-7]].

final_quiz.q: Which is one of the AIH's traits of a good SBT scenario?
options: It tests the learner against the ACS
It does not offer an obvious answer
It has one right answer you can grade
It sets up errors for her to catch
final_quiz.why: A good scenario is not a test, will not have one right answer, does not offer an obvious answer, should not promote errors, and should promote situational awareness and decision-making [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

final_quiz.q: How does the AIH suggest using an NTSB accident description as a case study?
options: Read the probable cause first to frame the talk
Use only reports on the learner's own airplane
Remove the probable cause and let learners discuss
Quiz learners on the dates and facts in it
final_quiz.why: Remove the NTSB determination of probable cause so learners can discuss it without bias, then share the NTSB's finding, which can lead to discussion of how to avoid that type of accident [[25:121|AIH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: Once your learner begins making decisions in a scenario, what role should you take?
options: Mentor and learning facilitator
Examiner who grades each decision
Pilot in command who decides for her
Silent observer who never steps in
final_quiz.why: When the learner begins to make decisions, the flight instructor should revert to the role of mentor and learning facilitator, and turn planning and execution over to the learner as soon as possible [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. You still keep safety: learners should never exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

final_quiz.q: How should the postflight review in this SBT lesson plan usually begin?
options: With your grade sheet for the flight
With a written test on the arrival
With a replay of your own notes
With the learner's self-critique
final_quiz.why: The SBT plan says the postflight review is a dialogue in which the instructor asks reflective questions, and typically the discussion should begin with learner self-critique [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. Collaborative assessment works the same way: self-assessment first, then the instructor's [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

takeaways: The teaching process has four steps: preparation, presentation, application, and assessment (review and evaluation). They stay the same whatever method you use.
Objectives and standards come first: a measurable description, conditions and criteria, with decision-based objectives as the learner advances.
Write every lesson plan down, keep its scope reasonable, and change or drop it in flight when the learner needs review.
Plan the flight as thoroughly as the learner does, and review the task on the ground before every flight.
Present with an introduction, a logical development and a conclusion that adds nothing new, and combine methods to fit the lesson.
Let the learner apply it right away and get it right the first few times; learner tells, instructor does is the key step.
Close every period with a review against the objectives, a record and a plan for next time; after a scenario, use collaborative assessment.
Problem-based learning uses real problems with no single answer: SBT, collaborative problem-solving and case studies, never trick tests.
cfi_notes: How it is tested: the evaluator selects at least Tasks E, F and G and one other from Area I (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I NOTE), so this Task is a possible fourth choice. The objective verb is describing, and evaluators should test application and correlation with scenario-based questions when possible (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Have one instrument lesson ready to walk through from preparation to debrief.

PTS words and 9B words: the PTS's fourth item, review and evaluation, matches AIH Chapter 7 and Figure 9-7 [[25:153|AIH 7-9]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], while Chapter 5 calls the same step assessment [[25:104|AIH 5-1]]. Both are correct; say both.

Source conflict: Chapter 5 gives demonstration-performance five phases, with learner performance and instructor supervision separate [[25:124|AIH 5-21]], while Chapter 9 gives four, combining them [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Both chapters say the two happen at the same time [[25:125|AIH 5-22]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Know both counts.

Source wording: AIH 9-6 says demonstration-performance can be applied to telling-and-doing 'in three steps' [[25:176|AIH 9-6]], yet Figure 9-7 shows preparation plus four tell-and-do rows [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The text describes three tell-and-do steps (instructor tells and does, learner tells and instructor does, learner tells and does) before evaluation [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Use the figure's sequence and name learner tells, instructor does as the key transition.

Problem-based learning appears twice in the AIH: as one of the training delivery methods [[25:113|AIH 5-10]], and as an approach with three types of instruction [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. So PBL belongs on your list of presentation methods too. The FOI Teaching Methods Task lists scenario-based training as its own item (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area I, Task D).

Overlap: in this Task, review and evaluation is the lesson-closing step of the teaching process. Critiques, oral questions, written and performance tests and collaborative assessment in depth belong to FOI.I.E, and each presentation method in depth to FOI.I.D. Give the process view first, then offer the detail if the examiner asks.

The PTS lists the ability to develop scenario-based instruction that meets lesson objectives, and to use learner-centered grading and debriefing, among what the evaluator checks (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). A good answer in this Task shows both.

Commercially developed lesson plans are acceptable on flight instructor practical tests [[25:153|AIH 7-9]], but be able to explain and adapt every line; the AIH encourages creativity when adapting preprinted plans to specific learners [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].
gaps: No source here gives a standard length for a ground or flight lesson, or how much time to give the briefing and the debrief. The AIH only says to plan time for the unexpected and not to plan too much for the time available [[25:105|AIH 5-2]].

The IFH Instrument Training Lesson Guide lists lesson content only; it gives no three-part objectives, completion standards or times for each lesson [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. The only standard is for the final lessons: review and practice until the student can consistently perform all required tasks to the practical test standards [[23:344|IFH B-3]]. You write the rest.

The AIH's SBT lesson plan and flight scenario examples are VFR (a nontowered airport arrival, a flight to a playoff game) [[25:155|AIH 7-11]] [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. No source here gives an instrument SBT lesson plan; the only instrument-specific hint is radio outages during visualization [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
No source says how many demonstrations to give before the learner tries a maneuver; the AIH says only to let the learner perform as soon as possible after a demonstration [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
The PTS references FAA-H-8083-9; this lesson uses only the current 9B, so any older-edition teaching process terms the 9B dropped are not covered here.

activities.title: True or false: application
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: You should take the controls the moment the learner makes a mistake.
cards.why: False. Safety permitting, it is often better to let learners go part way into a mistake and find a way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

cards.s: With a learner progressing normally, avoid too much assistance.
cards.why: True. Avoid unnecessary interruptions or too much assistance [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

cards.s: Application is an evaluation phase, so grade each error as it happens.
cards.why: False. It is a learning phase rather than an evaluation phase; correct errors in a positive and timely way [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

cards.s: A learner who flies a maneuver correctly may still not understand it.
cards.why: True. Have the learner vary it, combine it or apply its elements to other maneuvers [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

cards.s: Solo practice of a maneuver should come only after reasonable competence.
In a recovery, keeping the learner on the controls with you adds safety.
cards.why: False. Nothing is gained by having the learner on the controls and fighting for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

activities.title: Diagnostic, formative or summative?
activities.intro: Tap an assessment, then the kind it is.

items.t: IFH Lesson 1: ground and flight evaluation of a new student
Checking what a transferring learner knows before training starts
An ungraded wrap-up at the end of today's holding lesson
Tells you what to reinforce in the next lesson
A stage check at the end of the approach block
A chapter quiz on approach charts

activities.why: Definitions from [[25:132|AIH 6-1]]. IFH Lesson 1 is a ground and flight evaluation of the student's knowledge and performance [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

activities.title: One holding lesson, start to finish
activities.intro: You are the CFII for Ken, a private pilot with 150 hours in his fifth instrument lesson. Today the syllabus introduces holding at a VOR. Make each call.

steps.s: The night before, the syllabus objective reads: 'Ken will learn holding.'
options: Use it as written, since the syllabus is approved
Rewrite it with a behavior, conditions and criteria
Drop it and let the flight set the goal
Replace it with the ACS tolerances alone
steps.why: Objectives should be measurable, with a description, conditions and criteria [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:109|AIH 5-6]]. ACS standards cover only the most critical tasks, and the ACS is a testing tool [[25:108|AIH 5-5]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

steps.s: In the briefing, Ken says he read about entries last week and wants to skip the ground review.
options: Agree, and save the time for more holds
Skip it, but quiz him in the air instead
Do a short review on the ground first
Cancel and send him back to ground school
steps.why: Even with ground school done, review the task with the learner before flight [[25:174|AIH 9-4]], and a short review of earlier lessons is usually necessary in flight training [[25:152|AIH 7-8]].

steps.s: You demonstrate the first hold. What comes next?
options: Ken tells you each step while you fly the next
Ken flies five holds while you stay silent
You fly two more so he can watch closely
You move on to the approach to save time
steps.why: Learner tells, instructor does is the key transition: he organizes his thoughts and you check his understanding before he is busy flying [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Let him perform soon after the demonstration [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

steps.s: Ken now flies holds well at the VOR he trained on.
options: Grade him Perform and close the block
Repeat the same hold until the hour is up
Have him explain the entry rules once more
Assign a hold at a new fix with a new entry
steps.why: To check understanding, have the learner vary the maneuver, combine it with other operations, or apply it elsewhere [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

steps.s: Back on the ground, ten minutes remain.
options: You list every error and send him home
He replays and rates the flight, then you compare
You begin a new topic on DME arcs
You skip the debrief and log the time
steps.why: Review before the period ends [[25:126|AIH 5-23]] with collaborative assessment: self-assessment, then yours, then a comparison [[25:182|AIH 9-12]] [[25:136|AIH 6-5]]. Do not introduce new ideas in the conclusion [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].
